extracted.intended_audience: litigators, judges, and legal scholars handling unfair-competition/news-appropriation disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Legal criteria and equitable standards for recognizing and protecting news (information/dispatches) as a business commodity and preventing its unfair appropriation by competitors. Primarily for use in briefs and judicial decision-making about injunctions, trade-secrets-like protection, and the temporal scope of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as a business commodity is property
rubrics_metrics.description: News is property because it costs money and labor to produce and has commercial value for which others will pay; its sole elements of value are novelty, accuracy, and presence where and when people are interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that news lacks tangible form and intrinsic desirability but acquires commercial value through organization of vigilance, investigation, transmission and distribution (capital and labor). Treats raw event as material and the message as the product the creator is entitled to as property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership of the created message (exclusive right in one's own product)
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization that creates the commercial product (its own message from an event) has an exclusive right to that product; this right is limited to the message it itself has secured and created, not an unlimited monopoly on announcing the happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between ownership of one’s own dispatches/messages and a general monopoly on reporting an event; other organizations may have the same right in messages they themselves create.

rubrics_metrics.name: No right to appropriate another's created message
rubrics_metrics.description: A competing organization may not appropriate the message which another has secured and created by exclusive effort and expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames appropriation as theft of the product of another's expense and labor; supports equitable relief against surreptitious taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable protection against appropriation and unfair competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The property right in news is entitled to protection by equity (e.g., injunction) against every form of appropriation or unfair competition throughout the period of the news' distributing value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts of equity will restrain acts that injure the enterprise even where the immediate thing taken is intangible or not property in the narrow sense; equity looks to results and the injury to the business as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual and confidential relations afford additional protection
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to property and unfair-competition remedies, news shared with members or agents under contracts or relations of confidence is protected by those contractual/confidential rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where news is furnished to subscribers or members under contract/confidential understanding, that relationship can form an independent basis to enjoin appropriation; confidentiality and special-purpose holding can prevent abandonment of property rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property right does not expire upon mere first publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The property right in news does not disappear the instant news gets first publication (e.g., a single early paper or bulletin); it continues until the owner has realized the full commercial benefit of the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects rule that a single token publication dedicates the contents to the public; points to practical business realities (e.g., time-zoned distribution) and precedent holding that a short priority window suffices to 'gain its reward'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of protection is fact-specific (priority/'precommunicatedness')
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent/duration of protection is determined by the commercial value and circumstances — courts have allowed short priority periods (a few minutes for stock tickers; sixty minutes in National Telegraph) sufficient for the producer to gain its reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes the protected right as 'precommunicatedness' — the priority in communication — and urges courts to tailor the timeframe so the producer can realize the news' commercial value without destroying the business model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent collection/use is permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: A third party who independently collects the same facts by its own diligence and effort may legitimately use and publish them; the property right does not preclude independent gathering and utilization of the same materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that property in compiled news does not vest exclusive rights in the underlying facts; only surreptitious appropriation from the plaintiff's efforts is wrongful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential or contract-based disclosure does not necessarily abandon property rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts compiled and put in form for specific, confidential use remain property; supplying information to subscribers under contractual obligations does not automatically dedicate it to the public or destroy the owner's right unless abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites authority (F. W. Dodge) stating compilation held for a special/confidential purpose is still protectable; courts should consider whether publication constituted intended abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will protect intangibles integral to business success (goodwill, trade-secret-like collections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the immediate object taken (words, symbols, printed tape) is not property standing alone, when used as the means by which an enterprise achieves success those intangibles can be subject to equitable protection to prevent injury to the enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to trade names, franchises, good will and secret processes; equity acts to prevent appropriation that would remotely injure property interests of the business.

rubrics_metrics.name: No protection where the subject matter is tainted by illegality
rubrics_metrics.description: Property protection may be denied if the news or collection is so tainted with illegality that it is not entitled to protection (i.e., contraband or unlawful uses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges cases where courts refused protection because the material was so implicated in illegal activity that equitable relief would be inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy/practical necessity principle (to prevent parasitic free-riding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizes that protection is necessary to prevent parasites who would appropriate expensive collections and destroy the economics of news gathering; without such protection the business of gathering and distributing news could collapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses practical examples (time-zone disadvantages, early single-copy publication) to argue that immediate loss of exclusive commercial use would make large-scale news enterprises unsustainable and thereby harm the public interest.
